title: How AI makes video: inside the animated carousel
description: AI doesn't film anything. It writes a page that knows how to draw any instant, and the browser takes a picture 30 times per second. Step by step, with Clint's real carousel.

related.title: Clint Intelligence
related.body: In practice: Aura and the agents that show up in this tutorial's carousel.

blocks.text: You know those Instagram carousels where every slide moves, the messages arrive in time with the music and everything loops seamlessly? I always assumed that meant hours in After Effects. Yep. You can do it with AI, and the way it does it is very different from what I imagined.

In this series I'll show how I built a real animated carousel for Clint, from brief to MP4. In this first tutorial, the question is simple: how can an AI, which only writes text, deliver a video? Shall we?

items.label: Slide 1 of the Clint carousel, made by the AI with the rules from this tutorial.

blocks.text: AI doesn't film. It writes code

The first thing I had to understand: the model doesn't generate video pixels. It writes an HTML page, with CSS and a bit of JavaScript. That page has a function called seek(t). You pass in an instant, say 1.5 seconds, and the page draws itself exactly as it should look at that instant.

It sounds like a detail, but it changes everything. If the frame depends only on time, it's always the same. No timers, no animations running on their own, nothing random. I can ask for frame 45 ten times and get the same thing ten times. That's what keeps the video jitter-free and the loop seamless.

blocks.label: The idea in a few lines

blocks.text: Then the browser becomes a camera

With the page ready, Playwright comes in, a tool that controls the browser through code. It opens the page, calls seek(0) and takes a picture. Calls seek(1/30) and takes another. And so on: 30 pictures per second, 180 pictures for a 6-second slide.

At the end, ffmpeg stitches those pictures into an MP4 and lays the soundtrack on top. The soundtrack was also written in code, at 120 beats per minute. One beat every half second. That's why the messages arrive at 1.0 s, 1.5 s and 3.0 s: they land on the beat.
Without rules, AI animates like a robot

This is the point that made me write this series. If you just ask "animate this slide," the AI delivers something like this: everything moves in at constant speed and stops all at once, with no weight at all. It works, but it looks like a presentation from 2008.

items.label: Without rules: linear motion, no weight, no breathing room.
With rules: springs, a light squash and everything on the beat.

blocks.caption: Same page, same timings. The only difference is the motion curve. Both videos were rendered for this article.

blocks.text: Look at the one on the right. The messages arrive with a spring: they speed up, overshoot the mark just a tiny bit and settle. The bubble squashes slightly when it lands, as if it had weight. The background breathes. None of this is luck. Every detail came from a rule written before the AI started.
Want to understand why the spring feels like it has weight?
The step by step I followed

Who it's for, what each slide needs to say and what the CTA is. In Clint's case: a lead arrives on WhatsApp, the AI replies, it becomes an opportunity in the CRM, the meeting gets booked, Aura follows up and the carousel closes with "Start your free trial".
Every half second of every slide in a table: what appears, what moves, where the cursor is and which sound plays. It seems like overkill, but it's what leaves the AI no room to make things up.
Format, rhythm, curves, colors, what's forbidden. That file is the subject of the next tutorial.
One HTML file for each slide, each with its own seek(t).
Playwright takes the pictures, ffmpeg assembles them, and the soundtrack goes in normalized to Instagram's volume.
A sheet with one frame per beat, side by side. Looking at that sheet is where the flaws show up.
The result

blocks.caption: The 6 slides at 1080×1350, 30 frames per second, each with its own loop. Here on the blog they're in a reduced version so they load fast. Data and conversations are illustrative.

blocks.text: The rules the AI reads before it starts are here.

So, does it make more sense now? AI isn't a video editor. It's great at writing code that follows rules. The better the rules, the better the video. In the next tutorial I open the file where those rules live, CLAUDE.md, and show every flaw that turned into a line in it.

Credit to the people who opened this path for me: Movez's thread about animated carousels with AI and the work of Felipe Borges, who published the criador-de-carrosseis-simples skill. The links are in the sources below.
